answer: Age exerts a statistically significant negative influence on the likelihood of dissaving (withdrawing more money from savings than depositing). Specifically, as individuals age from young adulthood into their early thirties (ages 24–32), the likelihood and odds of dissaving decrease significantly (odds ratio ≈ 0.959 per additional year of age, p < 0.001; average marginal effect = -0.76 percentage points per year), both unconditionally and when holding income, BMI, gender, and race/ethnicity constant. When testing for non-linearity using a quadratic age specification, dissaving propensity peaks in the mid-twenties (~age 25.4) and follows a steep, accelerating decline through age 32. In the context of economic time preference, wherein dissaving serves as an empirical proxy for a higher rate of time preference (present orientation / impatience), increasing age is associated with a lower rate of time preference and greater future orientation / financial discipline.

payload.workflow: Inspected the NLSY79 dataset, evaluated empirical dissaving frequencies across ages 24 to 32, estimated bivariate and multivariable linear logistic regressions, tested quadratic age specifications (AGE and AGE_2), calculated marginal effects and odds ratios, and contextualized results in terms of economic time preference theory.
payload.hypothesis: Age has a statistically significant negative association with the likelihood of dissaving (withdrawing more money from savings than depositing), indicating that older individuals have a lower rate of time preference (greater patience and future orientation) compared to younger individuals, even after adjusting for income, BMI, gender, and racial/ethnic background.
